repeaters.empty: Import your area's repeaters from a file: they're saved on the device, work offline and are sorted by distance.

repeaters.simplex: Transmit on the same frequency (no offset, or not reported)
repeaters.toneNone: No tone reported: it may not use one, or the data is missing
repeaters.toneDigital: Digital mode: set with color code / talkgroup, not a tone

output.text: The frequency the repeater retransmits on: set it on your radio to listen.

input.text: The frequency the repeater listens on. Radios work it out if you set the offset.

offset.text: The difference between both: usually ±0.6 MHz on 2 m (VHF) and ±5 MHz on 70 cm (UHF). On the radio it's "shift" or "offset", with its + or − sign.

tone.text: A low tone your radio sends with your voice to "open" the repeater; without it you're ignored. On the radio it's "T", "Tone", "CTCSS" or "PL". DCS is an equivalent digital code.

mode.text: FM is the usual analog handheld mode. DMR, D-STAR or C4FM/Fusion are digital: they need a compatible radio and other settings (color code, talkgroup).

repeaters.report: Report it's not working or has wrong data
repeaters.importedNoPlace: {{count}} repeaters imported, but the town of {{missing}} wasn't found: they go last, without distance.
repeaters.importedApprox_one: {{count}} came without coordinates and was placed at the center of its town (approximate distance, with ≈).
repeaters.importedApprox_other: {{count}} came without coordinates and were placed at the center of their town (approximate distance, with ≈).
repeaters.importNone: No repeaters found in the file. Use a CSV, GPX or KML exported from RepeaterBook, or a CHIRP CSV.
repeaters.howTo: How to get them: sign up for free at repeaterbook.com, find your country (or your province or region), tap "Export" and download the file (CSV, GPX or KML). If it has no coordinates, each one is placed at the center of its town. A CHIRP CSV from your radio club works too. You can import several: they're added together.
repeaters.attribution: RepeaterBook data: "Data courtesy of RepeaterBook.com", for personal use. Confirm frequency and tone with the club before transmitting; transmitting requires a license.

radio.nacionalNote: AM reaches farther (hundreds of km at night); FM sounds better but only near the station. Frequencies: Radio Nacional (via Wikipedia); check them with your radio.
radio.nacionalNoteUY: Public radio: Radio Uruguay (AM 1050 in Montevideo) and its FM repeater network in the interior. AM reaches farther at night; FM only nearby. Frequencies: Radiodifusión Nacional del Uruguay (via Wikipedia); check them with your radio.
radio.nacionalTitleBO: Nearest Radio Patria Nueva (state radio) station

radio.nacionalTitlePE: Nearest Radio Nacional del Perú station
radio.nacionalNotePE: Public radio: Radio Nacional del Perú (IRTP), FM 103.9 and AM 850 in Lima and 70 FM stations across the country. AM reaches farther at night; FM only nearby. Frequencies come from IRTP's official list (from 2021): if yours differs, let us know.
radio.nacionalNoteCL: Chile has no national public radio: this shows the Radio Bío-Bío network (private, with stations in every region), which reports emergencies. fem.desc: Emergencies only: keep it clear. Monitor it whenever you are in the mountains. Once contact is made, move to 139.970 or 138.510 to talk.

free2.name: Free use · secondary
free2.desc: Another free-use channel, if 139.970 is busy.

csa.name: Cuerpo de Socorro Andino
csa.desc: Listed in mountain guides as the Chilean Andean Rescue Corps frequency; we found no official confirmation. Chile has no official mountain frequency: on the Chilean side of the Andes, also monitor 140.970.

rangers.name: Park rangers
rangers.desc: Monitored by the Aconcagua rangers and, according to mountain guides, other parks. There is no official publication: confirm it at the ranger station.

conaf.name: CONAF (Chilean park rangers)
conaf.desc: Listed on Wikiexplora as CONAF's; not confirmed. In Magallanes (Torres del Paine and Kawésqar), CONAF publishes 143.800 MHz: see "Park frequencies".

carabineros.name: Radio Club de Carabineros
carabineros.desc: Amateur radio repeater of the Carabineros radio club (not the police channel). Outside an emergency, transmitting requires an amateur license.

radio.emergencyOnly: Only if your life depends on it. Not free to use: outside a real emergency, don't transmit there.

peFree.title: Free-use radios (Peru)
peFree.intro: Family walkie-talkies: no license needed at 500 mW or less. They are for talking within your group, not for calling institutions.
peFree.note: Unconfirmed: from the MTC regulation (2012 version) and its official channel plan; we could not see the current frequency plan. Not for public services. European PMR446 radios (446 MHz) are not listed as free use in Peru, so we leave them out. The 27 MHz citizens band exists (up to 5 W, no protection from interference), but we found neither the procedure nor the channels. If anything does not match, tell us from Settings.

rener.title: Amateur radio emergency network (RENER, Peru)
rener.intro: RENER, run by the Radio Club Peruano with INDECI, is activated in emergencies and disasters. These are amateur radio frequencies: licensed operators transmit.

hf.name: HF 40 m: primary frequency
hf.desc: Local and international link. The secondary is 7,123 kHz LSB.

hf20.name: HF 20 m: international
hf20.desc: International primary; the secondary is 14,167 kHz USB.

indeci.name: RENER–INDECI link (HF)
indeci.desc: With Civil Defense. Also 7,415 kHz USB.

rpt1.name: Lima repeater (OA4O)
rpt1.desc: Primary. The temporary repeaters in Trujillo, Huaraz and Arequipa are linked and use the same frequency.

rener.note: With your life in danger you can ask for help by any means; otherwise, transmitting on these frequencies requires an amateur radio license (MTC). 155.640 MHz (INDECI) and 155.760 MHz (Peruvian Red Cross) circulate online, but the institutions do not publish them and they are for institutional use: transmitting there without authorization is an offence. That is why we do not list them. To ask for help by phone, INDECI answers on 115.
rener.sources: Source: RENER operating procedures manual 2024, Radio Club Peruano (oa4o.pe). The list is subject to change: confirm it with the radio club.

park.title: Park frequencies
park.intro: The ones each national park or protected area publishes for visitor emergencies, with their phones. First the park you are in; then the others that publish a frequency.
park.noRadioAR: The park doesn't publish a VHF frequency for visitors: with a radio, use the FEM, 140.970 MHz.
park.noRadioCL: CONAF doesn't publish a VHF frequency for this area: with a radio, monitor the Socorro Andino one or the FEM, 140.970 MHz.
park.noRadioBO: SERNAP doesn't publish a radio frequency for visitors in this area. Before going in, tell the rangers and bring a way to communicate; in an emergency, see Bolivia's numbers in Emergency contacts.
park.noRadioPE: SERNANP doesn't publish a radio frequency for visitors in this area. Before going in, tell the area office and bring a way to communicate; in an emergency call 105 (Police) or 116 (Fire).
park.othersTitle: Other parks with a published frequency
park.note: Park frequencies are for emergencies; coverage depends on the terrain. Before going in, register at the ranger station and ask which one they use in the area.
park.sourceOfAR: Administración de Parques Nacionales (argentina.gob.ar/parquesnacionales, CC BY 4.0), with each frequency's source; boundaries: IGN (CC BY 4.0).
park.sourceOfCL: CONAF (conaf.cl), with each frequency's source; boundaries: © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL).
park.sourceOfBO: Bolivia: boundaries © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL) and SERNAP contact (sernap.gob.bo).
park.sourceOfPE: Peru: boundaries from SERNANP (MINAM), simplified derived map, and its headquarters contact (gob.pe/sernanp).

radio.mountainNote: The FEM and the two free-use ones are free to use without a license under Resolution 5/2015 (in Argentina). Outside an emergency, transmitting on other frequencies or on the Chilean side requires the proper authorization. A radio does not replace calling 911, the ranger station or 131 if there is signal.
radio.mountainSources: Sources: Federación Andinistas Argentinos (FEM, 2021), Club Andino Mercedario (2024), Wikiexplora (Chile), Andesport and Meunier (park rangers). Confirm the ones for your area at the hut or ranger station and save them in "My frequencies".
radio.distressNote: Transmitting needs a radio for that band. Use them only when a life is truly at risk: a false call is a crime.
radio.hamText: Radio amateurs set up emergency networks when communications fail: in floods, earthquakes or fires they are often the ones passing information and calling for help. Listening needs no license; transmitting does. When life is in danger, international rules allow calling for help by any means.

hamLicense.AR: In Argentina the license is issued by ENACOM; Radio Club Argentino and local clubs run the courses (in the 2013 La Plata floods they kept communications going).
hamLicense.CL: In Chile the license is issued by SUBTEL after an exam; radio clubs prepare you for it and many run emergency networks.
hamLicense.UY: In Uruguay the permit is issued by URSEC; Radio Club Uruguayo (CX1AA) and local clubs run the courses.
hamLicense.BO: In Bolivia the license is issued by ATT (the telecom and transport regulator); Radio Club de Bolivia and departmental clubs run the courses.
hamLicense.PE: In Peru the license is issued by MTC; Radio Club Peruano (OA4O) runs the courses. Its emergency network (RENER) uses 146.520 MHz simplex.

radio.securityNote: The park ranger, CONAF and Radio Club de Carabineros frequencies are only for calling for help when a life is in danger: with a life at risk you may ask for help by any means. Gendarmerie and police frequencies aren't included: they aren't public and many are encrypted. Listening to forces or services without authorization may be a crime (in Argentina, Penal Code, art. 153).

maps.slopeHint: Terrain slope with the inclinometer colors, only above the snow line, computed from the area elevation (works offline if you downloaded it). Below the snow line, no color. It is a guide only: the model wind does not see how valleys deflect it, and neither slope nor wind tells whether the snow is unstable: check the local avalanche bulletin. With ~30 m elevation data, short very steep slopes may not show.

altimeter.disclaimer: GPS altimeter: it is not 100% accurate. GPS altitude is usually off by 10 to 30 m (much more than the position on the map) and gets worse under trees, in gullies or with few satellites. Calibrate it with a point of known altitude or with the map altitude and use it as a reference, not as the only input for safety decisions.

altimeter.alarmHint: Beeps, vibrates and notifies while this screen is open. Given the GPS error it may go off a few meters early or late.

about.gps: GPS computes altitude from the same satellites as the position, but the geometry makes it about 1.5 to 3 times less precise: with good signal, ±10 to 30 m.
about.android: Many Android phones report altitude above the GPS ellipsoid rather than above sea level: uncalibrated, in Argentina and Chile it can be off by a few tens of meters. Calibrating fixes it.
about.map: The map altitude comes from the offline maps' elevation model (about 30 m per point): it is ground level, good for calibrating on open terrain and unreliable at the foot of a cliff or on top of a building.
about.tips: For better readings: outdoors, holding the phone still for a few seconds, away from rock walls or buildings.
about.barometer: Once VikArg is an installed app (not web) it can use the phone's barometer, if it has one: it measures altitude changes to within 1 to 3 m, though it also needs calibrating because pressure changes with the weather.

declination.intro: Declination is the angle between true north (the one on maps and GPS) and magnetic north (where the needle points). It changes with place and over the years. It's computed offline with the World Magnetic Model (WMM).
declination.choosePlace: Choose a place above (your location, a waypoint or coordinates).
declination.dialLabel: True north up and magnetic north turned by the declination
declination.meaningW: The needle points {{value}}° to the left (west) of true north.
declination.meaningE: The needle points {{value}}° to the right (east) of true north.
declination.annual: It changes about {{minutes}}′ per year towards the {{side}}.
declination.error: If you don't correct it, you drift about {{meters}} m for every km you walk.
declination.modelExpired: The date is outside the WMM 2025 model (valid until {{until}}): the value is approximate. Update the app.
declination.bearingMag: Magnetic bearing (what the compass shows), in degrees
declination.bearingTrue: True bearing (measured on the map), in degrees
declination.mapIntro: The map margin gives the declination for the year it was made and how much it changes per year. Enter them to get today's value. If the map only shows a sign: + is East and − is West (you can type it with the number).

what.text: True (geographic): towards the pole, the one on maps and GPS. Magnetic: where the needle points. East declination = the needle is to the right of true north; West = to the left.

rule.m2t: Compass to map (magnetic → true): add East, subtract West.
rule.t2m: Map to compass (true → magnetic): subtract East, add West.

gmer.text: From Geographic (true) to Magnetic, East is subtracted (Este Resta), and West is added. The other way round it flips: from magnetic to true, add East and subtract West.

example.textW: With {{decl}}° West ({{where}}): the compass shows {{mag}}° → on the map it's {{true}}°. You measure {{true2}}° on the map → set {{mag2}}° on the compass.
example.textE: With {{decl}}° East ({{where}}): the compass shows {{mag}}° → on the map it's {{true}}°. You measure {{true2}}° on the map → set {{mag2}}° on the compass.

mapToCompass.s1: On the map, join where you are and where you're going with the edge of the baseplate (direction arrow towards the destination).
mapToCompass.s2: Turn the bezel until its lines are parallel to the meridians (map north up) and read the true bearing.
mapToCompass.s3: Convert it to magnetic with the rule above and turn the bezel to that value.
mapToCompass.s4: Holding the compass level, turn yourself (not the bezel) until the red needle sits inside the orienting arrow.
mapToCompass.s5: Walk where the direction arrow points, picking landmarks along that line.

compassToMap.s1: Point the direction arrow at what you see (a hill, a hut).
compassToMap.s2: Turn the bezel until the red needle sits in the orienting arrow and read the magnetic bearing.
compassToMap.s3: Convert it to true and set that value on the bezel.
compassToMap.s4: Lay the baseplate on the map with the bezel lines parallel to the meridians and the edge touching the point: you are somewhere on that line.

adjust.text: If your compass can be adjusted, set the declination once and it reads true bearings: don't also do the math, or you'll correct it twice. Check the setting every few years or when you change region.

grid.text: Maps with a grid (UTM or the IGN's Gauss-Krüger) have a third north, that of the grid lines. The difference from true north (convergence) is usually a few degrees and is printed in the margin. If you measure against the grid, use the map's grid–magnetic angle, updated with the annual change.

region.text: It varies a lot: about 7–12° West in northern and central Argentina, Buenos Aires and Montevideo, about 2° West in Mendoza, almost 0° in Santiago, about 5° East in Bariloche and 10–12° East in southern Patagonia. Everywhere it drifts West by about 5 to 13′ per year: a 30-year-old map can be several degrees off.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.device: Your data (inventory, documents, medical records, waypoints, tracks, garden) stays encrypted on your device and never leaves it.
privacy.server: If you turn on notifications, the VikArg server keeps just what it needs to alert you with the app closed: inventory expirations and shortages, and the alert locations rounded to 1 km (your waypoints with alerts, the garden, storage places and your last known location, which you can turn off in Settings → Notifications).
privacy.services: For weather, maps, nearby services and satellite images, the app queries public services (Open-Meteo, your server or OpenFreeMap, OpenStreetMap, NASA) with the coordinates of the area you're looking at, like any website. It doesn't send them your data.
privacy.choice: Anything else leaves only if you decide: a backup, moving your data to another device (encrypted with your password and deleted from the server after 24 hours), sharing with a family member or sending a report.
privacy.delete: To delete everything the server has about you: Settings → Delete my account.

zoneCountry.CL: Chile has no official home-garden calendar: the Argentine zone with a similar climate is used ({{zone}}).
zoneCountry.UY: Uruguay has no official home-garden calendar: the Argentine zone with a similar climate is used ({{zone}}).
zoneCountry.BO: Bolivia has no official garden calendar by crop and month (INIAF does not publish one). There are two estimated zones: "Bolivian valleys (Tarija)", built from an NGO manual, and "Bolivian tropics and Yungas", from a table of a cooperation project (12 crops); on the altiplano pick the closest one by hand and treat the months as a reference.
zoneCountry.PE: Peru has no official garden calendar by crop and month (INIA does not publish an open one): the climate of the coast, highlands and jungle matches no Argentine zone. There is an estimated "Peruvian highlands" zone (7 Andean crops, from the INIA highlands calendar); for the coast and jungle pick the closest by hand ("Bolivian valleys" is a temperate valley climate) and treat the months as a reference.

garden.zoneEstimatedValles: This zone comes from an NGO manual for the Central Tarija Valley (2016), not an official source: months were read from graphic tables and may be off by a month. It suits temperate valleys; on the altiplano or in the tropics the months change. Use it as guidance and check what is done locally.
garden.zoneEstimatedSierraPeru: This zone comes from the INIA Peru "Highlands agricultural calendar" (September to November; copied by hand from its publication, without the document at hand) and has only 7 Andean crops, rainfed. Harvest months were computed from each crop's cycle and change with altitude and variety (the higher, the longer the cycle). Use it as guidance and ask your local agricultural agency.
garden.zoneEstimatedTropico: This zone comes from a sowing table of a cooperation project for the Cochabamba tropics and the La Paz Yungas (Jatun Sacha, supported by UNODC): a single, unofficial source, not validated by INIAF. It does not tell direct sowing from seedbeds nor the Yungas from the tropics, and has only 12 crops. Use it as guidance and check what is done in your area.
garden.zoneEstimated: There is no INTA guide for this zone: the calendar is an estimate (mild frosts, very hot and humid summer). Use it as a guideline.
garden.coverNote: Under cover (greenhouse or tunnel) in this zone.
garden.missing: Not in this zone's guide: {{list}}. You can try them in a greenhouse.
garden.sources: ProHuerta planner (INTA, 2012). Crop manual for the organic family garden (Goites, INTA 2008, CC BY 4.0). Field crop calendar for northern Patagonia (INTA EEA Alto Valle). Sowing calendar for the lower Río Negro valley (INTA EEA Valle Inferior). Garden planner for southern Santa Cruz (INTA EEA Santa Cruz). Agroecological garden calendar for La Rioja (INTA EEA La Rioja). Sowing calendar for La Pampa (INTA EEA Anguil). Crop coefficients and evapotranspiration: FAO-56. Dates are approximate: every year and place is different.
